IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_01: Day 6. <LINE> <LINE> We got a stable response on the test bench today, after months of dead ends. It's stronger and more consistent than anything we ever saw come out of the trials with the pharmacological compound. For a second there I forgot to be careful about what that actually means. <LINE> <LINE> Next step is testing it on living tissue. We're going to need authorization for that, and a candidate. I keep thinking about who that's going to be. <LINE> <LINE> [On the back, in pencil: a sketch of the spinal shunt with two measurements crossed out and corrected.]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_02: SURGICAL & INITIAL ADAPTATION LOG: DAY 12 <LINE> DISTRIBUTION: PROGRAM OVERSIGHT <LINE> <LINE> Surgical coupling of prototype unit to Subject 01 completed without acute mechanical trauma. Biocomponent shunt successfully seated along the T8 to L2 vertebrae, integrating directly with primary spinal pathways. Autonomic synchronization confirmed: the bioelectric array is drawing baseline power directly from the host's metabolic glucose and ATP reserves as designed. <LINE> <LINE> Physiological response upon recovery was severe. Subject exhibited immediate, violent neuro-inflammatory rejection symptoms: localized spinal hyperthermia peaking at 103.4°F, involuntary muscular contractions along peripheral motor nerves, and acute radiating neuropathy. <LINE> <LINE> Standard induction protocol was initiated immediately post-op: a loading dose of clinical immunosuppressant, repeated every forty-eight hours, to blunt the host immune response and force cellular integration across the neural junctions. <LINE> <LINE> Acute phase contained after seventy-two hours of chemical suppression and mandatory bed rest. Inflammatory markers are receding, spinal tremors have resolved, and motor control diagnostics are steady. Subject remains on maintenance suppression until full integration, projected at several weeks. Cleared to begin light range-of-motion drills tomorrow, with first tactical live-fire trials scheduled for Day 19. <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENTS: spinal shunt blueprint, revision B (XXXXXXXX), with the T8 to L2 seat dimensioned; induction dosing sheet.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_03: FIELD TEST LOG: DAY 19 <LINE> DISTRIBUTION: PROGRAM OVERSIGHT <LINE> <LINE> Subject completed first live tactical trial outside bench conditions. Protocol: reactive close-quarters live-fire drill, implant active, results benchmarked against subject's established baseline. <LINE> <LINE> Target acquisition and room clearance completed in 0.72 seconds. Four reactive silhouettes neutralized with center-mass hits before the first spent brass casing hit the concrete floor. High-speed footage at 240 fps confirms the subject repositioned between targets while the rifle's cycling mechanism was still ejecting the initial round. <LINE> <LINE> Subject self-reported the activation as disorienting but tolerable, quote on file. Operational implications for room clearance and counter-ambush exceed prior projections. Recommend proceeding to next test phase per existing schedule. <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENTS: unit blueprint, revision B, with activation curves noted in the margin; 240 fps tape.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_04: I asked him what it actually felt like in that room. <LINE> <LINE> He told me it felt like the world got polite all of a sudden and started waiting its turn. He said he watched dust motes hanging almost still in the air, like they were caught in amber. He knocked an empty mug off the briefing table on purpose, watched it sink toward the floor like it was falling through water, and caught it an inch above the tiles without rushing. <LINE> <LINE> I laughed when he told me. He didn't. He looked at his hands and told me: "The problem isn't while it's running, doc. The problem is when it stops, and the rest of the world slams back down on your head all at once." <LINE> <LINE> Later, to lighten the mood a little, I asked him why he had signed up for the program. We almost never ask: every candidate is military personnel who enrolled in the experimental program of their own free will. He took a while to answer. He said it was for the extra money. That he had promised his girlfriend he would take her to the moon, and that with what this program pays, someday he would be able to afford it. He said it without embarrassment, the way you'd give someone an address. I couldn't tell if he was serious. It didn't seem to matter. <LINE> <LINE> I don't know why those two things are staying with me more than the numbers are. <LINE> <LINE> [On the back, in pencil: the logic matrix blueprint copied from memory, with an arrow and the words "what does it feel like?"]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_05: PROGRESS REPORT: WEEK 6 <LINE> DISTRIBUTION: PROGRAM OVERSIGHT <LINE> <LINE> Implant performance continues to exceed theoretical models. Latency between visual stimulus and neuromuscular execution shows an unprecedented drop, down to sub-10-millisecond thresholds. <LINE> <LINE> The bioelectrical draw on the subject's cardiovascular system is significant but currently manageable within prescribed operating windows. <LINE> <LINE> Behavioral observation: between sessions, the subject frequently asks when the next activation will be. Nursing staff report finding him twice in the test room after hours, sitting in front of the powered-down control bench. When asked about it, he stated that "it's easier to think in there." <LINE> <LINE> Recommend maintaining current pace rather than accelerating, pending further physiological data. <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENTS: logic matrix blueprint, revision C; control firmware listing, version 2.1, burned into the unit's EPROM. Thermal cut-off correction pending approval.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_06: INCIDENT REPORT: SEVERE ADVERSE EVENT <LINE> DISTRIBUTION: PROGRAM OVERSIGHT XXXXXXXX <LINE> <LINE> Subject was scheduled for a high-intensity stress trial: six consecutive room-clearing breach runs across a four-hour window, testing the viability of holding activation past the unit's thermal safety cut-off, as requested by XXXXXXXXXXXX. Runs 1 through 5 yielded record marks, with the subject overriding the cut-off on every run and neutralizing thirty reactive targets across the full tactical course without a single miss. <LINE> <LINE> On run 6, during entry through breach point delta, subject suffered an acute neuro-motor collapse. Video feed records the primary weapon slipping from subject's hands mid-stride, followed by severe lower-limb ataxia and a violent fall against the doorframe. Subject was found conscious but incapacitated, presenting with epistaxis, acute cephalalgia, and uncontrolled tremors in both upper extremities. <LINE> <LINE> Protocol was aborted immediately. Subject required manual evacuation from the killhouse. Tremors and cognitive lag persisted over six hours post-event. Subject quote on file: "It's like something inside me keeps running after I've already stopped." <LINE> <LINE> Formal classification logged as Minor Neurological Fatigue to prevent schedule interruption, pending internal review. Recommend pacing reduction. <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENTS: unit blueprint, revision C, with the thermal cut-off marked in red; footage of run 6. <LINE> <LINE> [Handwritten at the bottom, in a different hand: "Received. Classification approved. Schedule stands."]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_07: I sat with him in medical for three hours after they carried him out of the killhouse. <LINE> <LINE> I handed him a paper cup of water. His hands were shaking so hard the water splashed over his knees, over the cot, over my clipboard. He couldn't grip it. He looked down at his fingers, breathing like a wounded dog, and tried to force his thumb to touch his index finger. He couldn't do it. The micro-grid in his spine was still firing stray pulses down his arms, twitching his tendons like loose strings. <LINE> <LINE> He hooked my sleeve with his forearm, since his fingers wouldn't close, and looked right at me. "Look at this, doc. I can't even hold a cigarette. My brain is telling my fingers to close, but they're vibrating like high-voltage wire. What did you put inside me?" <LINE> <LINE> I told him it was just lactic acid and temporary neural fatigue. I told him a good night's sleep would fix it. I lied straight to his face because I was terrified he'd start screaming and someone outside that door would hear him. <LINE> <LINE> Then I walked back to my desk and wrote 'Minor' at the top of the official incident report. I hate myself for it. I know exactly what I'm doing, and I hate myself for it. <LINE> <LINE> [Stapled to the back: the unit blueprint, revision C. Over the thermal cut-off, handwritten: "we overrode this ourselves".]

IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_08: CLINICAL NOTE: IMMUNE SUPPRESSION & TRANSITION PROTOCOL <LINE> DISTRIBUTION: PROGRAM OVERSIGHT <LINE> <LINE> Following yesterday's collapse, subject presents with localized spinal inflammation, lumbar rigidity, and an intermittent fever spiking to 102.8°F. Blood panels indicate an acute systemic immune reaction directed at the vertebral junction. <LINE> <LINE> While the subject reached full integration some time ago, the high-frequency test runs have re-inflamed the neural pathways, provoking a secondary immune response. The clinical immunosuppression protocol has been re-initiated at full dosage. Fever broke within twelve hours and spinal swelling has subsided. <LINE> <LINE> SUPPLY ISSUE: the clinical compound is the contractor's property and cannot be manufactured on base. The last shipment arrived at a third of the requested amount, with no date for the next one. At the current rate, stock covers a single subject on maintenance, not the three planned. <LINE> <LINE> Until further notice, doses are RATIONED: full coverage only during early adaptation and as a rescue after severe overheating. Any request for doses outside that schedule goes through me. Urgently requesting that the contractor restore deliveries before Subjects 02 and 03 are implanted. <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENTS: vertebral interface blueprint, revision C, with inflammation points marked; clinical compound stock sheet; listing of the CRI cooling program for the EPROM, test version: cuts out sooner and cools almost twice as fast.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_09: Not going to write this one up for anyone else to read. <LINE> <LINE> The subject no longer says he wants to continue. Last night he asked me, practically begging, to pull him from the program. Said he isn't sleeping. Said he sometimes hears things that aren't there. I told him we'd evaluate it. I didn't tell him I already know what the evaluation is going to say, because the numbers from this past month are already telling me. <LINE> <LINE> Moving forward anyway. Someone above me is also moving forward, and I don't know if I have real room to say no. <LINE> <LINE> [On the back, in pencil: the listing of a program for the unit's EPROM, labeled CMP. In the margin: "make the unit adapt to the body, not the body to the unit". Below, underlined twice: "is it enough?" Nobody asked for it. Unsigned.]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_10: 03 asked me about 01. <LINE> <LINE> They crossed paths yesterday in the infirmary hallway, the morning of his surgery, while 01 was being taken to the exam room: sedated, in a wheelchair, between two orderlies. He says 01 looked at him like he wasn't there, and then smiled at him. He wanted to know if that was normal. He wanted to know if 01 is all right. <LINE> <LINE> I told him 01 is under observation. That's true. I didn't tell him the observation wing now has a door that locks from the outside, or what had to be cleaned off the training room floor on Tuesday, or why the night orderly asked for a transfer. <LINE> <LINE> Then he asked me if it was true that 01 had a girlfriend. I said yes. He asked me if she knows. <LINE> <LINE> I didn't know what to tell him. <LINE> <LINE> 01 is getting no treatment. The order from above is to document the full curve: sedatives so he doesn't hurt himself or anyone else, and nothing more. I asked to try full suspension and full immunosuppression on him. I was told the compound doesn't stretch far enough to waste on a subject who is already lost. If 02 starts the same way, I'm not asking permission. <LINE> <LINE> With 01 I didn't ask. Last night, while he slept sedated, I burned the CMP program I wrote on the back of my papers into his unit. No order, no record. The idea is for the unit to settle into him instead of fighting him, so that every time it fires during a crisis it burns him a little less. I don't know if it will work. I have no way to measure it without them finding out upstairs, and I can't tell if what I'm seeing is the program or what I want to see. If anyone checks his unit's EPROM, they'll find my code. <LINE> <LINE> 01 doesn't talk about the moon anymore. He barely talks at all. When he does, he counts. Numbers, under his breath, like he's measuring something we can't see. I asked him what he was counting and he said: "How long you all take, doc." <LINE> <LINE> 03 went into surgery at nine. The signature is mine. <LINE> <LINE> [Stapled to the back: the blueprint of Subject 03's unit, revision D, with my approval signature.]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_11: DISCHARGE REPORT: SUBJECT 02 <LINE> DISTRIBUTION: COMMAND OVERSIGHT ONLY <LINE> <LINE> When Subject 02 showed the first signs of the curve observed in Subject 01 (insomnia, voices, extreme irritability), the remission protocol was applied for the first time, without prior authorization from command: full suspension of activation, mandatory rest and full immunosuppression, despite the rationing. <LINE> <LINE> The protocol worked. Within eleven days the tremors subsided, the auditory hallucinations stopped and neurological markers returned to acceptable values. It was the first result of its kind in the entire program. <LINE> <LINE> In parallel, the subject developed a progressive flattening of affect: he stopped eating in the mess hall, stopped talking to staff, stopped leaving his room. He asked several times to go back to the test room. Subject quote on file: "Without the unit, everything moves at your speed. And it's all gray." <LINE> <LINE> Subject 02 was found dead in his room at 05:40 on XX XXXX. Cause was recorded as self-inflicted. The body remains in the medical wing's cold storage, implant in place, pending transfer authorization XXXXXXXX. <LINE> <LINE> Subject 01 remains under observation and sedation, without treatment, as ordered. <LINE> <LINE> Recommend that any future remission protocol include psychiatric follow-up. <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENTS: Subject 02 medical history; blueprint of the implanted unit, revision D. <LINE> <LINE> [Handwritten in the margin: "We got him out of the cyberpsychosis. We didn't know how to get him out of the rest."]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteTitle_12: Final note, cut off (military researcher, official)
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_12: FINAL PROGRAM MEMORANDUM: DRAFT <LINE> DATE: JULY 6, 1993 <LINE> DISTRIBUTION: COMMAND OVERSIGHT ONLY <LINE> <LINE> Formally recommending indefinite suspension of the project. <LINE> <LINE> Following the deterioration of Subject 01, two additional candidates (Subjects 02 and 03) were implanted and rotated through the tactical evaluation cycle. Both subjects confirmed the identical clinical curve: initial unmatched operational lethality, followed within days by severe motor tremors, persistent insomnia, violent auditory paranoia, and irreversible neural degradation. The forced remission of Subject 02 halted the neurological decline; the outcome is recorded in the attached discharge report. The implant operates flawlessly; the human nervous system simply cannot sustain the operational tempo this program demands of it. <LINE> <LINE> Medical staff cannot continue trials. A severe fever broke out in the lower residential quarters this morning, and half my technical team is currently bedridden with sudden respiratory distress and nausea. <LINE> <LINE> I need to submit this report so I can finally go down to quarters and rest, my head feels impossibly heavy and I can barely keep my eyes op
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_13: Third time this month depot B's count doesn't add up. Items on the sensitive-materials log are missing, but the system says nothing went out of here. Flagged it twice already, told both times to recheck, that it's probably a loading error. <LINE> <LINE> Rechecked. It's not a loading error. On that week's access sheet there's a signature I don't recognize, with a service number that isn't on the personnel roster. <LINE> <LINE> Putting this in writing, just in case. Not because I think something's going to happen, but because if it does, I don't want to be the one who said nothing.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_14: Got called upstairs today. Odd questions, none of them direct. "Who had access to depot B these past weeks." "Did you notice anything unusual in the transfers." Answered what I knew, which isn't much. When I went to show them the signature, that week's sheet wasn't in the folder anymore. <LINE> <LINE> Got the feeling they already know something I don't, and that maybe it's better that way. Not going to keep asking around. I've got enough on my plate without getting into something that clearly isn't mine to solve.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_15: Got my transfer. Effective Monday, signed by someone I've never seen, no reason given. "Needs of the service." <LINE> <LINE> My replacement starts counting depot B from scratch, on new sheets. Whatever happened before doesn't exist on any paper anymore, except this one. <LINE> <LINE> Half the shift is in the infirmary with a fever, so nobody's going to notice me leave. I'm leaving this note under the drawer of the guard desk. Not sure who for. Whoever comes to count after me, I guess. <LINE> <LINE> If that's you: make sure to count and check three times.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_16: I can't believe what I found in the storage archives behind the robotics annex. An unlabeled archival box tucked away behind surplus project crates. No department stamps, no accession numbers, no manifest of any kind: just a thick stack of technical drawings and schematics, clearly never meant for a college syllabus. Half the pages are faded photocopies of photocopies, sections are missing or redacted, but what's here is enough to prove it's real. Not theory. A functional biocircuit designed for a living human spine. <LINE> <LINE> I hooked the primary logic array to an oscilloscope in lab 3 after hours. Stimulus in, motor pulse out: barely twelve milliseconds end to end on an unloaded bench. Obviously that's in isolation, without biological impedance or neural feedback, but a trained sprinter needs well over a hundred just to react to the starting gun. Whoever drafted this wasn't trying to improve human reaction time; they were trying to delete biological delay altogether. <LINE> <LINE> I'm not going to tell the faculty adviser about this. If he sees these files, he'll turn them over to the dean or throw them in the incinerator. I have to see if I can build one that works. <LINE> <LINE> [Stapled to the back: photocopies of the blueprints, with the logic matrix highlighted in yellow. The control code pages are nearly black from being photocopied so many times: none of it is legible.]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_17: Prototype 01 and 02 are complete write-offs. <LINE> <LINE> Built 01 using salvaged bus controllers and breadboards from the engineering scrap bins. Hooked it to a bench power supply; the capacitor bank melted into slag in less than two seconds. Needed proper thermal dissipation and a pulse limiter. <LINE> <LINE> Prototype 02 was worse. Slipped down to the animal holding facility at 2 AM and hooked it to a test rat. Complete disaster. The signal wasn't dampened, and the current fired every motor nerve in the poor thing's body all at once. Violent, instantaneous spasms. Died before it could take a single step. Had to dispose of the carcass in the incinerator before the morning shift arrived so nobody would notice the missing count. <LINE> <LINE> I can't do this alone without getting caught. Let my lab partner, Leo, in on it. He thinks I'm insane, but once he saw the latency figures on the scope, his jaw dropped. We're fabricating Prototype 03 tonight with a custom voltage regulator. <LINE> <LINE> [On the back: the Prototype 03 voltage regulator blueprint, drawn by hand over a photocopy of the original.]
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_18: LAB LOG: PROTOTYPE 03 RUN <LINE> <LINE> Set up an old VHS camcorder on a tripod in the basement vivarium to record the trial at maximum tape speed. Subject: adult lab rabbit fitted with prototype 03 on an exterior spinal harness. <LINE> <LINE> Triggered the pulse. The animal crossed the four-meter pen and cleared the partition before the video tape even registered the departure. On playback, there is a single smeared frame at the starting block and then the animal is already pressed against the opposite wall. The raw velocity works. Leo had named the rabbit Roger, after Roger Rabbit, his favorite movie, and spent the whole recording telling it "easy, champ" from behind the tripod. <LINE> <LINE> But the biological reality hit us like a brick. The animal collapsed immediately after. Heart rate skyrocketed past four hundred beats per minute, with severe lumbar tremors. <LINE> <LINE> Those blueprints didn't have a single word of medical caution in them. Just cold hardware specs, circuit traces, pinouts. Whoever designed this only cared about the machine, not what it does to living tissue. We had to raid the organic chemistry stockroom for anti-inflammatory compounds and solvents just to stabilize the animal's spinal swelling. Leo stayed with it all night, on the vivarium floor. He didn't say a word all the next day. <LINE> <LINE> If we're ever going to scale this up to a human harness, we need a reliable chemical stabilizer. <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENT: pulse limiter blueprint, first version, in pencil. Leo wrote "for Roger" in one corner.
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_19: LAB LOG: COMPONENT REFINEMENT <LINE> <LINE> Prototype 04 failed bench calibration. It had a micro-fracture in the bus trace, invisible to the naked eye, that opened up with heat: as soon as the unit warmed up, the pulse grounded out where it shouldn't have and burned out the neural interface board and the power cell. The whole workshop smelled of burnt plastic. The rest looks sound, but we have no spares for those two parts and no time to redo the trace, so we tossed it in the scrap bin under the lathe. Fabrication of Prototype 05 is underway; we managed to mill three functional units using the CNC lathe in the basement workshop. The first two came out identical; on the third the bit wandered and the bus trace came out thinner, so it heats up sooner than the others. It works, but it stays as a spare. All three carry the pulse limiter we designed after the rabbit. It eats into thermal headroom, since they run hot and cut out early, but it should keep the pulses from overloading the host's nerves like they did with the rabbit. <LINE> <LINE> Sourcing the chemical stabilizer has become our biggest bottleneck. One line in the parts list calls for an "integration agent" by supply code only. No name, no formula, no dosage. Whatever it is, we have zero access to it. Leo and I spent three nights distilling a crude substitute using laboratory-grade analgesics, pure ethanol, and a synthetic reactant stolen from the locked biochemistry cabinets. <LINE> <LINE> Bench assays show our homemade mixture underperforms the original specifications by at least half, and the impurities will definitely cause stomach cramps and nausea. But it slows the inflammatory cascade enough to keep neural tissue from burning out. I'm writing the whole synthesis down in the lab notebook, step by step, in case one of us isn't around to remember it. Three units of Prototype 05 ready on the bench, and doses for only two in our lockers. We hid the spare in the lab stockroom, wrapped in a lab coat. <LINE> <LINE> TO DO: <LINE> Return the biochemistry cabinet key before Monday. <LINE> New VHS tape (Leo taped a ball game over the rabbit one; says it was an accident). <LINE> Endurance test for the limiter: does it hold more than ten seconds straight without cutting out? <LINE> Get another animal to test the 05 on. Something bigger than a rabbit. <LINE> More electronics scrap and a spare power cell, in case another one burns like on the 04. <LINE> [crossed out] Test the 05 on <LINE> <LINE> ATTACHMENTS: Prototype 05 blueprint with the bus trace redrawn thicker because of the 04; on the third copy, handwritten, "spare".
IGUI_Sandevistan_NoteText_20: Everything fell apart in less than ten minutes. <LINE> <LINE> Emergency sirens started screaming across campus just after nine at night. Campus security blared an evacuation over the PA, but before we could pack our bags, the building's emergency lockdown kicked in. Security doors mag-locked, ground floor sealed. We're shut inside the science building. <LINE> <LINE> I looked out through the second-floor library window toward the parking lot. It's not a riot. It's a slaughterhouse. People are tearing each other apart with their teeth. I saw Professor Vance get dragged down by three students under a streetlight. Blood all over the windshields. <LINE> <LINE> Leo took the first unit of Prototype 05 and his dose of the compound, trying to find a service hatch on the north roof. I've got the second unit right here on the lab bench. The third is still hidden in the stockroom; there's no dose for it, and neither of us had the nerve to take it. I rigged the mechanical surgical guide to clamp against my mid-back, aligned directly along my spine. <LINE> <LINE> There is banging on the stairwell fire doors downstairs. The glass is cracking. I don't know if this thing is going to tear my nervous system to shreds, but if I have to break through that lobby and run through the campus, I need to be faster than whatever is waiting in the dark. <LINE> <LINE> Aligning the spinal shunt needles now. God help me. <LINE> <LINE> [Taped to the back: the last sheet of blueprints, with the surgical guide drawn in a hurry and the measurements of my own spine written by hand.]

IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page1_Text: A Sandevistan is a spinal implant that slows the world around you: zombies inside its bubble (about 16 tiles) crawl at a fraction of their speed while you run and strike faster. <LINE> <LINE> ACTIVATE: press the activation key (default Z; change it in Options > Mods > Sandevistan). Press it again to cut the implant off. The floating panel and the Implant tab of the character window show Heat, Neural Load, rejection and adaptation.
IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page2_Text: Every second the implant is on builds Heat. At 100 it cuts out on its own (a thermal cutout) and stays locked until it cools to 0. A manual shutdown is free and keeps your Heat. <LINE> <LINE> Higher adaptation levels lower the heat rate and cool you faster. Each overdrive collapse lowers your Heat ceiling (a thermal scar) by a few points; it recovers with time and sleep.
IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page3_Text: Using the implant builds Neural Load. From 60 you get symptoms: screen glitches, nosebleeds, the neural monitor complaining. At 80 cyberpsychosis sets in: whispers, blackouts, fury, terrors at night. Rest and antidepressants lower it. <LINE> <LINE> The only way out of cyberpsychosis: remove the implant and spend 5 days without any. The first 2 days are rough: stress and fatigue creep up. It leaves a neural scar: the next implant loads a bit faster. <LINE> <LINE> In a fury (cyberpsychosis) your melee weapons wear twice as fast. <LINE> <LINE> Adaptation lowers the load each use adds (up to -25%% at stable adaptation). Immunosuppressant coverage lowers it further and doubles how fast it decays.
IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page4_Text: Your body rejects the implant. Untreated, rejection climbs and at 100 the implant is destroyed (about three days). Immunosuppressants cover you while active: Clinical 48 h, Homemade 24 h (nausea, and it can fail) and Herbal 8 h (it accumulates toxicity). <LINE> <LINE> Each unit holds 3 doses: use them from the inventory menu. <LINE> <LINE> The dose option shows what it will do before you take it (rejection before and after, hours of coverage). Coverage also lowers the neural load each use adds. <LINE> <LINE> THE DOWNSIDE: each dose lowers your defenses (immunodepression, the broken-shield moodle). While coverage lasts it stays above a floor (clinical 50); afterwards it falls on its own in a few hours, slower if you are sick. With low defenses wounds get infected more and heal slower, and colds and spoiled food hit harder: disinfect, bandage cleanly and keep antibiotics at hand. Stacking doses (shock dosing) cuts neural load even more, but each extra dose lasts less and, if you overdid it, a rejection rebound comes when it ends.
IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page5_Text: The Sandevistan Adaptation skill grows with use and unlocks stronger slowdown, lower Heat and faster cooling. Lab prototypes (P05 and the homemade P06) cap at level 5; military grade goes up to 10 and is the most stable. <LINE> <LINE> Wear makes an implant run hotter: a worn one can be calibrated (Electrical 3 and First Aid 4). <LINE> <LINE> While the implant is on, climbing fences, windows and walls and bump stumbles stop failing with a chance equal to your adaptation; at stable adaptation (level 5 lab, 7 military) they never fail. <LINE> <LINE> Hover over a level square of the skill in the Skills tab to see exactly what that level gives, including how long the Overdrive lasts (lab up to 4 s, military up to 7 s).
IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page6_Text: Installing needs a scalpel, a suture needle (or a sewing needle and thread), disinfectant and a mirror (or standing in front of one); someone else can operate on you and you can operate on them (they choose whether to accept). Removing it is a longer, riskier surgery. <LINE> <LINE> You can also extract the implant from an ex-subject's body with a scalpel: the more First Aid you have, the less worn it comes out (First Aid 4 or more: perfect). With only a knife it is rougher: extra wear, twice the time and a chance to cut your hand.
IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page7_Text: The Sandevistan tab of the crafting menu has the synthetic compound, the immunosuppressants, the homemade Black Lace and the five parts (neural board, thermal regulator, power cell, chassis and harness) of Prototype 06. Notebooks and reports teach the recipes; the part quality you craft sets the prototype's wear. <LINE> <LINE> Each part needs a single skill (board and cell: Electrical; regulator: Welding; chassis: none, it takes more materials; harness: Tailoring) and the assembly only First Aid, so on a server everyone can specialize and trade parts. Studying an implant teaches you its design, and with paper and a pen you can write blueprints to teach it to others. The military implant can be replicated too (Mk. II): you need to study a working military unit while carrying both military dossiers complete, and build the parts (a military-grade microchip that can be built with lots of work).
IGUI_Sandevistan_Guide_Page8_Text: The implant takes up to two software chips: a System one (how it handles Heat, neural load and rejection) and a Skill one (what it lets you do). An empty slot is the usual behavior. To install a chip: right-click it in the inventory (10 seconds, with the implant off). Every change adds 3 rejection and leaves the implant recalibrating for one game hour (Heat rises 10 %% faster). To look at or remove the installed chips: right-click the equipped Sandevistan or the floor, in the Firmware menu; if your implant is explanted, the chips come back to your inventory. <LINE> <LINE> Programs are written: you need a blank chip (built with Electrical 4, or found now and then in electronics shops, laboratories and offices) and a computer with power, or a portable terminal (it cannot be built: you find it in military places) which uses one battery per program. It does not ask for Electrical: it is code. What counts is how used to the implant you are: each program occurs to you when you reach a given adaptation level (the Implant tab tells you how many you know and at which level the next one comes) and writing it takes less the more adapted you are (60 down to 25 seconds). Military designs (the Cryo Chamber) also ask for a military microchip. <LINE> <LINE> A chip that comes already programmed (very rare: laboratories, army depots and the military base) can be installed right away or decompiled on a computer with power or with the terminal: you learn the program even if your level is short of it, and the chip is left blank. Carrying both complete military dossiers also teaches Cryo Chamber.

IGUI_Sandevistan_FwDesc_Reactor: The counterpart of the Cryo Chamber. It turns the implant into a heat reservoir: the Heat bar still goes from 0 to 100, but it fills as if it went to 150 (everything moves 1.5 times slower), so you can stay on for much longer stretches. In exchange, with the implant off it cools at half the usual rate on top of that, and recovering from a full bar takes about three times as long. Thermal inertia: the momentum of continuous use builds 50 %% faster and fades at half the speed once you switch off.
